objective: Explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object.
subject: Science

sequence.next: Air resistance: why a feather DOES fall slower on Earth

vocabulary.meaning: A pull between the Earth and everything on it.
A push or a pull. You cannot see one. You see what it does.

vocabulary.in_use: I let go. Now it is unsupported.

steps_to_success.text: Say that gravity is a pull, not a push.
Explain that gravity pulls everything towards the Earth.
Use evidence to explain why a heavy thing and a light thing land together.
Explain whether things fall slower on the Moon.

spine.prompt: What do you already know about forces?
spine.plan_suggestion: Write up what the class gives you, in their words. Do not tidy it. You need the word PULL on the board before the next slide.
expected: A force is a push or a pull.
Forces make things speed up, slow down or change direction.
You cannot see a force. You see what it does.
spine.going_further: Give me a force you cannot see.

spine.prompt: I drop a pen. Why did it fall?
spine.plan_suggestion: Write up what they say, in their words. Do NOT correct it. Almost every class gives you some version of 'because it's heavy'. You will come back to this exact sentence at the end.

demonstration.fallback: Two water bottles, one full and one empty. Almost impossible to release unevenly.

shape.what: Drop the pen. Collect the wrong answer.
shape.how: Write their words up. Do not correct.
Say the sentence, THEN drop. Never both at once. Silence during.
You are showing them a mind working. Fill the Turn with them.
"We are changing our minds. That is what scientists do."

success_looks_like.model: We thought heavy things fall faster. We dropped a book and a pen and they landed together. So gravity pulls the same on everything.
success_looks_like.why: Old idea, evidence, new idea. Three moves, in that order, and the old idea is honoured rather than erased.
success_looks_like.minimum: The class can say what changed their mind, not just what the right answer is.

live_moves.do: Offer one yourself. "Someone told me it fell because it is heavy. Are they right?"
live_moves.why: You cannot turn a misconception you have not surfaced, and a silent class still holds it.

live_moves.see: A child's expression does not change during the drop.
live_moves.do: Note who. Ask them directly: "what did you expect to happen?"
live_moves.why: They have explained it away. This is the child the hinge will catch, and you can catch them first.

live_moves.see: They are copying the Turn frame instead of watching.
live_moves.do: "Pens down. Watch me. You will write it after."
live_moves.why: A child copying is not a child thinking, and the modelling is the point of these ten minutes.

live_moves.do: Say so, out loud. "That was my fault, not the science. Watch again."
live_moves.why: A teacher who admits a failed demonstration is modelling exactly what this lesson is about. Pretending it worked teaches them evidence does not matter.

if_stuck: Point at the thing while you name it. Drop the pen and say 'gravity pulled it down' at the moment it lands.
Do not simplify the science. Simplify the sentence.
if_finished: "You said the book is heavier. So why did they land together?" Let them sit in the contradiction.

spine.instruction: A marble and a ping-pong ball. A book and a shoe.
spine.plan_suggestion: Scribe what they say, then sharpen it with them. If a child says 'but a feather falls slower' - yes, and tell them to ask you next lesson.
expected: It does not matter how heavy. Gravity pulls the same on both.
spine.going_further: Does gravity pull harder on the book than the pen? How do you know?

shape.how: Predict on whiteboards. Stop. Drop. Stop. Now explain. Three separate moments, never overlapping.

shape.what: Pair two. They lead, you prompt.
shape.how: Same three moments. You are only asking 'why?'
Hands off. This is the last rung before independence.
'Gravity pulls the same on both.' Get it said, by them, out loud.

success_looks_like.model: They land together every time. It does not matter how heavy they are, because gravity pulls the same on both.
success_looks_like.why: Three rungs, and your hands come off at each one. By pair three they are doing the reasoning and you are silent. If you are still leading at pair three, the independent task will fail.
success_looks_like.minimum: They can predict, watch and explain as three separate steps without you chunking it for them.

live_moves.see: They predict AFTER seeing the result.
live_moves.do: Cover the objects. "Whiteboards up BEFORE I drop." Commit first, always.
live_moves.why: A prediction made after the event is not a prediction, and the surprise that changes minds only works if they committed.

live_moves.see: The same three children answering every time.
live_moves.do: Whiteboards up together, on three. Everybody commits, nobody hides.
live_moves.why: Guided practice with four voices is not guided practice. It is a demonstration with an audience.

live_moves.see: You are still leading at pair three.
live_moves.do: Stop talking. Ask 'why?' and wait. Count to five in your head.
live_moves.why: If your hands have not come off by the third rung, they are not ready for the independent task and it will fall over.

live_moves.see: A child says 'but a feather falls slower'.
live_moves.do: "Yes. And that is exactly what we do next lesson." Write their name down.
live_moves.why: They are right, they are ahead, and the honest answer respects that. Do not smuggle air resistance into today.

live_moves.see: They are explaining the result by weight again.
live_moves.do: Do not correct. Go bigger: the heaviest and lightest things in the room. Drop again.
live_moves.why: The misconception survives one demonstration. It rarely survives an extreme one.

if_stuck: Let them hold both objects. A child who has felt the difference and still seen them land together has an anchor no explanation gives.
Chunk harder: predict, stop, watch, stop, explain. Never two at once.
Take the explanation orally. You are removing the writing, not the thinking.
if_finished: "Find me two things in this room that will land together. Prove it."
"Does gravity pull harder on the book than the pen? How do you know?"

spine.instruction: Vote. Then write one sentence saying why.

hinge.scenario: On the Moon there is no air.
hinge.question: An astronaut drops a hammer and a feather. Same height. Same moment. Which lands first?
hinge.why_diagnostic: The Moon removes air resistance entirely, so a child cannot explain the result away. A child who still says hammer has not shifted; they have simply gone quiet.

spine.going_further: On the Moon gravity is weaker. So do things fall slower there?

spine.instruction: A friend says: heavy things fall faster.
spine.task: Write a reply that changes their mind. Use the evidence from today.
spine.going_further: Why DOES a feather fall slower than a hammer on Earth? Answer without saying gravity is weaker on the feather.

shape.what: Think and plan. No writing yet.
shape.how: Talk it through with a partner. What are you going to say first?
You are circulating. This is where the live moves below happen.

shape.what: Read it back. Improve ONE sentence.
shape.how: Not tidy it. Improve it. Which sentence is doing the least work?
Class judges one thing only: is the evidence doing the work?

success_looks_like.model: You might think heavy things fall faster, but actually they do not. When we dropped the book and the pen they landed at exactly the same moment. This is because gravity pulls the same on everything, however heavy it is.
success_looks_like.why: It names the wrong idea, contradicts it, gives the evidence we saw, and then explains the mechanism. Four moves. That is the whole shape of a scientific argument.
success_looks_like.minimum: Evidence from today, plus the word gravity doing something. 'Because of gravity' on its own is a word, not an idea.

live_moves.do: "You have told them they are wrong. Now tell them WHY. What did you SEE?"
live_moves.why: They have made a claim with no evidence. The claim is the easy half.
They have the word, not the idea. This is the single most common outcome and it looks like success.

live_moves.see: A retelling of the demonstration with no claim.
live_moves.do: "That is your evidence. Now what does it PROVE?"
live_moves.why: The opposite problem. Evidence with nothing hanging off it.

live_moves.see: They have written that the pen is lighter so it should fall slower.
live_moves.do: Do not correct it. "Show me on the board what happened." Let the memory do the work.
live_moves.why: This child has not turned. You need to know that, and telling them hides it.

live_moves.see: Half the class still blank at five minutes.
live_moves.do: STOP the class. Take ONE good opening sentence from a child, put it on the board, restart. Cost: one minute. Saves the other ten.
live_moves.why: Fifteen minutes of a child not knowing how to start is fifteen minutes wasted, and you will not get it back.
They were offered, not assigned. A child who does not need them should not use them.

if_stuck: "What happened when I dropped them?" Then: "that IS your evidence."
Let them say the whole thing aloud to you before they write a word.
Scribe their first sentence. They write the rest. You have removed the starting, not the thinking.
if_finished: The going further question on the slide.
"Now write the reply your friend sends back. What would they still argue?" This is much harder and it is the best thing you can give an early finisher.
Swap with a partner. Find the sentence doing the least work and say why.

spine.prompt: This is what we wrote at the start. Fix it.
spine.plan_suggestion: Write their opening sentence back up, word for word. Then: 'Is it right? Fix it.' They rewrite it themselves. Do not do it for them.

exit_ticket.question: Why did the pen fall?
exit_ticket.success_criteria: Must contain the word 'gravity' AND say what gravity DOES. 'Because of gravity' on its own is a word, not an idea.

teacher_key.support: Same thinking. Chunked instruction, oral route, stems offered to all.
teacher_key.secure: Gravity named as the cause, not just the word said.
teacher_key.further: Air resistance, without misattributing it to gravity.

first_thing: "Three things you know about forces. Whiteboards. Thirty seconds. Go."
"Right, hands down, shout them at me."
"Is a force always a push? Thumbs up for yes, down for no."
show_them_how: "I am going to drop this pen. Watch. ... Why did it fall?"
"Say that again. I am writing exactly what you said."
"Good. Leave it there. Now watch. I am going to drop TWO things."
"There is a pull between the Earth and every single object. It pulls YOU, which is why you are in your chair and not on the ceiling."
build_it_together: "Predict first. Whiteboards. Which one lands first?"
"It does not matter how heavy. So what IS gravity doing?"
quick_check: "On the Moon there is no air at all. None."
"Vote. Now write me ONE sentence saying why."
their_turn: "A friend says heavy things fall faster. You are going to change their mind."
"Use what we SAW today. Not what you think."
last_thing: "Look at what we wrote at the very start."

first_thing: Whiteboards and pens out on every table before they come in.
Sit beside the children who freeze at a blank whiteboard. Do not supply an answer.
A child writing nothing. That is often not daring, rather than not knowing.
show_them_how: Practise the drop three times. Both objects must leave your hands at the same instant.
Stand at the BACK and watch faces during the drop. The children whose expression does not change are the ones explaining it away.
Nothing during the drop. The silence is what makes it land.
build_it_together: Pairs with a big obvious mass difference. A book and a shoe.
Take a pair to the children who are unsure and let them do it themselves, twice.
quick_check: Read over shoulders as they write. Tell the teacher, quietly, roughly how many said hammer.
If more than a third say hammer, the teacher needs to know BEFORE they move on. That is your job in this minute.
their_turn: Read the stems aloud with them. Do not write for them.
Do not tell a child their reply is wrong. Ask what evidence they used.
last_thing: Who is nodding without saying anything? Those are tomorrow's starters.
Note the children whose sentence still says heavy. They have not turned.

yes: Generate five more retrieval questions on Y3 forces if this class needs longer.
no: Do not have AI answer the retrieval questions. Reading an answer is worth nothing.

yes: Find the Apollo 15 hammer and feather clip, for AFTER they have voted.
no: Do not show a video instead of doing it live. A child can dismiss a video. They cannot dismiss a book landing on the floor.
Do not have AI explain gravity. You are modelling the thinking.

yes: Build a quick prediction poll so every child commits before they see the result.
no: Do not use a simulation instead of the real objects.

yes: Sort the written sentences into gravity answers and no-air answers, so the split is visible instantly.
no: Do not use AI to mark the hinge. That decision is a professional judgement and it is the whole point of a hinge.

yes: Generate three more misconception prompts for children who finish early.
no: Do not let AI write the reply. The reply IS the assessment.

yes: Capture the before and after sentences into the tracker.
no: Do not upload children's work with names visible. SEQUENS never needs a name.

first_thing: A blank whiteboard is frightening if you are unsure. Cue a memory: 'what did we do with the springs?' Do not supply the answer.
Take it orally. You are retrieving forces knowledge, not handwriting.
show_them_how: 'Unsupported', 'attract' are abstract words for an invisible thing. A child can understand gravity perfectly and be unable to say it.
Point at the thing while you name it. Drop the pen and say 'gravity pulled it down' at the moment it lands.
Do not simplify the science. Simplify the sentence.
build_it_together: Predict + watch + explain is a working-memory load. Chunk it absolutely. Predict. Stop. Watch. Stop. Explain.
Let them hold the objects. A child who has felt both has an anchor no explanation can give.
quick_check: Do not give an easier hinge. An easier hinge diagnoses nothing.
Take the sentence orally. You are removing the writing, not the thinking.
Do not help them get it right. A wrong answer is the most useful thing that will happen today.
their_turn: They are the structure of a scientific argument. Using them is practising the move, not avoiding it.
'The evidence is...' - because they know what they SAW but not that it counts. Ask: 'what happened when I dropped them?' Then: 'that IS your evidence.'
last_thing: Say it to a partner before writing it.
A child who says 'gravity' but cannot say what gravity DOES has learned a word, not an idea.

needs: Sustained attention is the barrier
Thirty seconds is perfect for this child, and it is why the task is timed. Do not extend it.
Uncertainty is the barrier
'Three things' is precise and finite. Do NOT change it to 'as many as you can'.
Time to think is the barrier
Give the question, then wait five seconds in silence before taking answers.
first_thing.eal: This is a recall task. Accept 'push' in any language, accept a gesture, accept a drawing. Write the English word next to their answer; do not correct them into it.

needs: Hearing you is the barrier
Say the sentence, THEN drop. Never both at once - their eyes cannot be on your face.
Seeing it is the barrier
Say it aloud as it lands. Let them hold the book and pen first.
Uncertainty is the barrier
Say what is about to happen before you do it. A sudden bang is not a surprise, it is an ambush.
show_them_how.eal: This lesson turns on the word PULL, which is not an obvious word for a force in every language. Give the word, show the action, use it every time.

needs: Holding several things at once
Chunk absolutely. Predict. Stop. Watch. Stop. Explain.
The motor demand is the barrier
Pair them, or handle the objects for them. The motor demand is not the objective.
build_it_together.eal: 'Predict' is abstract. Say 'what will happen?' instead - concrete, same meaning. Let them answer with a gesture.

needs: Uncertainty is the barrier
A closed question with three options is exactly right. Do not soften it into 'what might happen?' - vagueness is harder, not kinder.
Hearing you is the barrier
The vote is visual. Make sure the three options are written, not just spoken.
quick_check.eal: The question depends on understanding 'no air'. Check that phrase specifically - not the science, the phrase.

needs: Reading or writing is the barrier
Offer a scribe. The objective is constructing an explanation, not spelling it.
Open-ended is the barrier
Give it a shape: 'four sentences, one for each starter.'
Social framing is the barrier
Reframe factually: 'write the correct explanation and the evidence for it.'
their_turn.eal: The stems are the most valuable thing in this lesson for an EAL child, and they are not a reduction. This is academic English, transferable to every science lesson they will ever have.

needs: Fear of being wrong is the barrier
Frame it as the class's sentence, never one child's. 'WE wrote this. WE are fixing it.'
Holding it in mind is the barrier
The original sentence must be visible, not remembered. That is why you write it back up.
last_thing.eal: Accept a partially correct English sentence with a fully correct idea. You are assessing the science.

first_thing: 'Give me a force you cannot see.' Asked to the room.
show_them_how: 'You said the book is heavier. So why did they land together?' Let them sit in it.
build_it_together: 'Does gravity pull harder on the book?' Ask it to the room and let it hang.
quick_check: 'On the Moon gravity is weaker. So do things fall slower?' Genuinely surprising, and genuinely true.
their_turn: 'Why DOES a feather fall slower on Earth?' Forces them to separate two forces they have treated as one.
last_thing: 'If gravity pulls the pen towards the Earth, does the pen pull the Earth?' It does. Let them leave with that.
